newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Berne comes under pressure to join Holocaust fund.
newsitem.headline: Berne comes under pressure to join Holocaust fund.

text.p: Pressure mounted on the Swiss government on Thursday to contribute to a Holocaust memorial fund set up by Switzerland's three biggest banks.
Government officials said they were working on a decision as quickly as possible.

But commentators across the political spectrum urged Berne to stop hesitating and declare how much it would give after the banks' decision on Wednesday to launch the fund with 100 million francs ($70 million).

Thomas Borer, special ambassador in charge of coordinating Berne's response to Holocaust questions, told Reuters the government was already working at speed on guidelines for a fund it may later join and which will include the bank payment.

"It was always our express will and intention to deliver what was asked of us as soon as possible. We will be discussing the concept of this fund with all interested sides in the next few days and weeks, including Jewish groups," Borer said.

But he reiterated the Swiss cabinet's official line that it would only decide whether and how much to pay after a panel of international historians presented its first findings on Switzerland's wartime role as a financial centre.
"It is not enough to want to 'decide before summer'," wrote the leading conservative daily, the Neue Zuercher Zeitung (NZZ), referring to the government's timing for a decision.
"What the Federal Council (cabinet) must now deliver is a statement of intent that it will create a Swiss humanitarian fund for victims of genocide and human rights violations," the NZZ said.
On the liberal side, Zurich's Tages-Anzeiger agreed. "The government is therefore going to have to act faster than it wants to," the newspaper wrote.

Swiss public radio RSR said the major banks had set an example by announcing their contribution on Wednesday, drawing applause from their most vocal critics led by world Jewish groups and U.S. Senator Alfonse D'Amato.
"The political authorities today must resign themselves to jump on the train that is already in motion and cooperate (in the fund)," the French-language radio said.

Seizing the initiative after months of public battering from Jewish groups, the three pillars of Swiss finance -- Union Bank of Switzerland (UBS), Credit Suisse Group and Swiss Bank Corp (SBC) -- invited the Swiss government and central bank to join the fund.

Jewish groups accuse banks of hoarding unclaimed wealth of Holocaust victims and demand compensation from Swiss authorities for having bought stolen gold from Hitler's central bank and turned away thousands of Jewish refugees as the Holocaust raged.

But politicians in Berne said the cabinet would probably not be rushed into any decision before the mid-year findings from the historical panel, which it needs in order to tell voters the money is being spent based on facts rather than allegations.
"The cabinet is worried about being accused of wasting tax money at a difficult time for the economy," one politician close to the government told Reuters.

In order to dodge the danger that a popular referendum could be called against a federal role in the fund, the decision to take part and how much to pay must be carefully prepared for domestic voters and parliament, the politician added.

The government and the private sector agreed last month to draft guidelines for using contributions from banks, insurers, machine tool makers and other companies who may have profited from Holocaust victims or trade with the Nazis.
"The decision on what the money will be used for and who are the beneficiaries will come in the next couple of weeks," Borer's spokeswoman said.
